analysis.title: China is becoming Japan — with worse imbalances and better cards
key_insights: Alicia Garcia Herrero (Natixis) argues China increasingly resembles post-bubble Japan, but its domestic imbalances are larger and its external position is stronger. She concludes that combination makes prolonged Japanese-style stagnation more likely.

Yao Yang, former dean of Peking University's National School of Development and a long-time critic of the 'Japanification' thesis, now says he is 'not that confident anymore about opposing that view'.

Chinese growth fell from 14% in 2007 to around 5% today, at least officially. Nominal growth has run below real growth because the GDP deflator is negative. Producer prices have fallen almost continuously since the property bubble burst in mid-2021.

The PBOC, like the BOJ before it, has eased slowly and reluctantly, keeping real rates high while the economy runs below potential. Fiscal support has been timid, partly because the debt sits with local governments.

The 10 trillion RMB (US$1.4 trillion) package of November 2024 was mostly a swap of hidden local government financing vehicle debt into official bonds. The report calls it useful for financial stability but not stimulus.

Yao's diagnosis is that the centre has squeezed local finances too hard and tighter political discipline has left officials unwilling to take initiative. The report compares this to Japan's zombie problem, with local governments and their financing vehicles that can neither invest, nor pay, nor fail.

China's savings rate stayed around 45% of GDP from the 2000s into the early 2020s. Japan's was around 33-35% at the equivalent stage and fell below 30% within a decade. Chinese household consumption is below 40% of GDP, while Japanese private consumption never fell much below half of GDP.

China's excess savings go abroad as goods. Its trade surplus exceeded US$1 trillion in 2025. Its surplus is almost entirely trade with negligible net investment income, unlike Japan, so it is more exposed to protectionism.

First offsetting difference: no Plaza Accord is available for the renminbi. China has capital controls, a weak currency and showed with its 2025 rare-earth export controls that it can retaliate. The US is more polarised and has raised tariffs on allies as well as rivals, which weakens its ability to build a coalition.

Second offsetting difference: China diversified toward the Global South. Its sales to ASEAN alone now exceed those to the US, versus close to 40% of Japanese exports going to the US in the mid-1980s. Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America absorb a growing share of Chinese EVs, machinery and steel.

Third offsetting difference: China is closer to the technological frontier, competing with the US in AI models, batteries, EVs, solar, telecom equipment and drones, and narrowing the gap in semiconductors despite US export controls.
IMF research finds Chinese total factor productivity growth declined during the slowdown, and frontier breakthroughs coexist with ruinous price wars in the same sectors.

The report argues China's external strengths may entrench the imbalance: with no Plaza Accord and the Global South as an outlet for its surplus, there is much less pressure to raise household consumption.
The outcome depends on whether China introduces structural reforms, the future of the US as global hegemon, and whether the Global South keeps supporting China's rise rather than fearing it.

tension_points.bull_case: China has stronger external cards than Japan did: no Plaza Accord is available, the US is weaker and more polarised, Chinese exports can go to the Global South (ASEAN sales now exceed those to the US), and China is closer to the technological frontier. Yao Yang expects a more stable equilibrium with the US eventually.
tension_points.bear_case: China's domestic imbalances are larger than Japan's (savings around 45% of GDP, household consumption below 40% of GDP, trade surplus above US$1 trillion). The external strengths may substitute for domestic reform, making prolonged stagnation more likely.
tension_points.what_invalidates: China introducing the structural reforms needed to avoid the Japanese fate, such as measures that address precautionary saving (pensions, health coverage, hukou-linked urban services).

theme_stances.key_argument: China's larger domestic imbalances combined with a stronger external position make prolonged Japanese-style stagnation more likely.
theme_stances.evidence: That combination makes a prolonged Japanese-style stagnation more likely, not less.

theme_stances.key_argument: External strength becomes a substitute for domestic reform.
theme_stances.evidence: External strength becomes a substitute for domestic reform.
